---
title: "Physical-Process Foccused (2PF) MLWP Seminar Series"
---

<a id="top"></a>

The Physical-Process MLWP Seminar Series is intended as a lightweight forum for
scientific exchange on machine-learning weather prediction through the lens of
atmospheric processes and physical consistency.

The aim is not to promote one model architecture or software framework. The aim
is to ask what current MLWP systems can and cannot represent physically, and how
we can learn from successes, failures, and targeted diagnostics.

I have also written an introductory blog post about the motivation for the
series [here](posts/2026-08-13-announcing-the-physical-process-mlwp-seminar-series/).

**If you want to be informed about upcoming talks** you can join the `2pf-mlwp`
mailing list by sending email to
[2pf-mlwp-request@freelists.org](mailto:2pf-mlwp-request@freelists.org?subject=subscribe)
with 'subscribe' in the Subject field OR by visiting the [mailing list
page](https://www.freelists.org/list/2pf-mlwp).

## Talk Series

> The general plan is that talks will be on the third Thursday of every month
at 11:00 Copenhagen time (CET in winter, CEST in summer), with a duration of 1 hour. It is planned that talks will be
recorded and made available on the seminar series website.

### Gergely Bölöni (DWD) {#gergely-boloni-dwd}

**Title:** Towards a machine-learning enhanced nowcasting tool for thunderstorm severity analysis and prediction

**Authors:** Gergely Bölöni, Paul James, Michael Debertshäuser, Susanne Theis

**Recording and slides:** [Watch the recording on YouTube](https://youtu.be/MjZJWwi7vP4) | [Download the slides (PDF)](https://cloud.denby.eu/s/cnsb5YQ2Ckj9TLC/download)

**Abstract:**

At the German Weather Service (DWD), the NowCastMIX system (James et al., 2018) is an important tool for issuing severe weather warnings on the next-hour timescale using radar, lightning, NWP, and other data. In its analysis step, NowCastMIX detects thunderstorm cells and assigns a severity level based on remote sensing and numerical model data at their locations. In the prediction step, the thunderstorm cells are clustered and then linearly extrapolated according to estimated motion vectors, with the extrapolated clusters retaining the severity assigned in the analysis step.

In order to improve the prediction step, we present a machine learning (ML) approach that aims at non-linear propagation and a representation of the convective life cycle of thunderstorm cell clusters. Our ML-approach is inspired by 2D fluid dynamics, i. e. convective storm development is treated as a forced 2D advection problem. A proof of concept and stages of the ML-model development will be shown through idealized experiments with synthetic data, followed by a demonstration with real data.

### Marvin Kähnert (MetNo) {#marvin-kahnert-metno}

**Title:** A first assessment of process-representation in Bris

**Recording and slides:** [Watch the recording on YouTube](https://youtu.be/Qld2ady8nvM) | [Download the slides (PDF)](https://cloud.denby.eu/s/Qw8Dd3x67gZ7z5T/download)

**Abstract:**

This talk presents a process-based evaluation of the ML weather prediction model Bris. Instead of focusing on conventional verification metrics, selected case studies of cold-air outbreaks (CAOs), stable boundary layers (SBLs), and persistent fog are analyzed. A deeper analysis of a CAO case investigates whether Bris reproduces the spatial coherence and organised structures of the event, providing first insights into how well the model represents atmospheric processes beyond pointwise forecast skill.

### Michael Denhard (DWD) {#michael-denhard-dwd}

**Title:** Error amplification in the AICON MLWP model

**Abstract:**

The global machine learning model AICON at DWD runs operationally at 13km horizontal resolution with a model time step of 3h. Goecke et al. (2026) show that its pressure field forecasts are inferior to the ICON NWP reference. The reason is that AICON amplifies noise during iterative forecast inference, because there is no fine-tuning rollout training with longer forecast lead times. In the DA cycle, where background model forecasts provide a first guess for the next analysis, the autocorrelation property of the background dynamics also transports errors through time. AICON ranks these errors as predictable variance based on its 3h model training. This leads to a noise amplification property in the most strongly autocorrelated parameters like the pressure field. We explore the error growth in the AICON operational ML model with Singular Vectors and further analyze the autocorrelation properties of the ICON-DREAM and ERA5 re-analysis datasets. From these results we derive recommendations for a longer-range rollout training process.

### Francesco Pasquini (KNMI) {#francesco-pasquini-knmi}

**Title:** Assessing the ability of a stretched-grid deep-learning weather prediction model to capture physical balances

**Abstract:**

Weather forecasting has traditionally relied on Numerical Weather Prediction (NWP) models, which simulate weather by solving the governing fluid equations. Recently, the emergence of Deep Learning Weather Prediction (DLWP) models has opened a new era in weather forecasting, offering a data-driven alternative to classical NWP approaches. Regional DLWP models such as the stretched-grid model Bris developed by Met Norway have demonstrated performance on par with, or even slightly better than, regional NWP models across a range of standard forecast metrics. By overcoming the coarse horizontal resolution that constrained earlier global data-driven models, the operational use of regional DLWP systems now appears increasingly promising.

Nevertheless, the performance of such models during extreme events is generally inferior to that of regional NWP models, and comprehensive evaluations of their ability to generate physically realistic forecasts are still lacking. Here, we present a study comparing the physical consistency of the deterministic version of Bris with the control run of the operational MetCoOp Ensemble Prediction System (MEPS) in forecasting the severe extratropical cyclone Poly, which hit the Netherlands on 5 July 2023. We examine whether Bris accurately represents deviations from key atmospheric balances and whether it reproduces expected dynamics of the storm.

We show that, despite its relatively good performance in terms of RMSE, Bris struggles to capture important mesoscale features of the event and that it significantly disrupts several atmospheric balances. This unrealistic disruption is mainly linked to the fine-scale noise evidenced in its output fields, which leads to incorrect and unrealistic spatial gradients. These results raise critical questions for improving AI-based models to better represent extreme events and how to ensure physical consistency in their predictions.

### Gabriel Moldovan (ECMWF) {#gabriel-moldovan-ecmwf}

**Title:** Improving the representation of light precipitation in AIFS-Single v1 through non-negativity constraints

**Abstract:**

Graph neural network-based models such as AIFS and GraphCast have been shown to represent precipitation with an intense drizzle bias. In this work, we show that this behaviour is related to gradient ambiguity arising at the zero-precipitation boundary when training with MSE. By simply enforcing non-negativity on the total precipitation head, we show that the model learns a substantially different representation of precipitation. More specifically, the resulting geometrical boundary at the zero-precipitation threshold allows the model to use the negative-output region as a proxy for dryness, while eliminating the gradient ambiguity at zero precipitation.

## Guiding Questions

Each seminar should try to answer:

- What physical process is being studied?
- What model, dataset, architecture, training setup, diagnostic, or constraint
  is being tested?
- What was the hypothesis for improving or evaluating representation of the
  process?
- What were the findings?
- What might transfer to other MLWP settings?
- What remains unresolved?

## Candidate Themes

- Convective initiation and precipitation organisation.
- Cloud and precipitation physics.
- Physical consistency and conservation constraints.
- Geostrophic balance, stability, waves, and dynamical consistency.
- Extremes and rare events beyond pointwise scores.
- Spatial structure and object-based verification.
- Generative and probabilistic models: are sampled structures physically
  meaningful?
- Physics-based constraints and regime separation, for example dry versus
  slight-rain conditions.
- Data assimilation and latent-state representations.
- Architecture choices from a physical-process perspective.

## Participation

The series is still being formed. Suggestions for speakers, papers, topics, or
examples are welcome. See [Contact](contact.qmd).
